newsitem.title: FRANCE: BNP late with 7 bln Ffr in repos - paper.
newsitem.headline: BNP late with 7 bln Ffr in repos - paper.

text.p: Banque Nationale de Paris was two days late honouring the return leg of repurchase agreements, or pension livree, involving seven billion francs of French government bonds, French daily La Tribune said on Monday.

La Tribune also said some of the bank's counterparties had accused the French bank of not borrowing the bonds in question to fulfill its contractual obligations because it would have cost more than delaying the return of the bonds.
BNP officials were not immediately available for comment.
Philippe Bordenave, head of capital markets at BNP, was quoted as saying BNP made a mistake anticipating the shortage of bonds available at the end of 1996.
Despite making use of bonds retained by the Treasury for special circumstances (Fonds de Soutien des rentes), including short-term repo trades, it did not have enough bonds.
"The result: we were short about seven billion francs. And we were only able to deliver on January 2, two days late," Bordenave said.
The paper said BNP lost out on 1.3 million francs of interest on money it had lent to counterparties in exchange for the bonds.
But it quoted one banker as saying this was a tenth of the losses the bank would have incurred by reborrowing the bonds elsewhere to return them on time.

La Tribune said BNP had borrowed 7.25 percent April 2006 and 8.50 percent 2008 government bonds, or OATs, a month earlier via a repurchase agreement in which they agreed to return the securities at a pre-agreed price on December 31.

La Tribune also said, "according to our information," tapes of conversations held by Credit Agricole, the main counterparty in the repo transactions, showed it had offered BNP the bonds it needed at market prices.

It became apparent there were some liquidity problems at the end of the last year when the Treasury issued on December 27 nine billion francs of 2008, 2011 and 2012 government bonds and said they would be available for use in short-term repo trades.

Jean-Daniel Cohen, president of Louis Dreyfus Finance and head of a "peacemaking" committee set up to look into the episode, told Reuters its main objective was to find out exactly what had happened and to see how a similar situation could be avoided in the future.
Cohen said the Tribune article had already taken the matter forward considerably, and it was not certain the conclusions reached by the committee would be made public.
He said any decision about whether there would be further compensatory payments would be made bilaterally between the counterparties involved, and he did not want to prejudge the outcome.

He said it was "an excellent sign of the maturity of the market place" that all the parties involved had agreed without any pressure to abide by the conclusions reached. He declined to say which other institutions were involved.
